args.text: --- title: 'Hello World' description: 'Change the FHE computation in the default template so that the E3 returns two times the sum, and run it again.' --- import { Callout, Steps } from 'nextra/components' import { Flow, LinkCard, LinkCards } from '@/components/ui' # Hello World In this tutorial you'll change the FHE computation in the default template and run the E3 again. It's meant for developers who've already been through the [Quick Start](/build/quick-start). Once you're done, your E3 hands back 2 × (a + b) instead of plain a + b, and you'll know which files hold the computation, its test, and its labels in the client. ## Before you begin You'll want the `my-first-e3` project from the [Quick Start](/build/quick-start), just as it was, nothing changed. Every one of the paths on this page is relative to the project folder. ## How the template computes The whole FHE computation lives in the one Rust function, `fhe_processor`, in `program/src/lib.rs`. Everything else in the template is just ferrying ciphertexts to this function and carting its result off to the committee. 1. The client encrypts each number with the committee public key, then calls `MyProgram.publishInput`. 2. As soon as the input window closes, the coordination server (`server/index.ts`) reads the published inputs and fires them off to the program server on port 13151. 3. The program server (`.interfold/support/dev/src/main.rs`) calls `fhe_processor` and sends the encrypted result straight back to the coordination server. 4. The coordination server publishes the encrypted result, and the committee decrypts it. Here's what the default computation in `program/src/lib.rs` looks like. We've pulled out the doc comment above `policy` here: ```rust filename="program/src/lib.rs" use e3_compute_provider::{FHEProcessorInput, InputPolicy}; use fhe::bfv::Ciphertext; use fhe_traits::{DeserializeParametrized, Serialize}; pub fn policy() -> InputPolicy { InputPolicy::default() } /// Implementation of the CiphertextProcessor function pub fn fhe_processor(fhe_inputs: FHEProcessorInput<'_>) -> Vec { let mut sum = Ciphertext::zero(fhe_inputs.params); for (bytes, _) in fhe_inputs.ciphertexts { let ciphertext = Ciphertext::from_bytes(&bytes, fhe_inputs.params).unwrap(); sum += &ciphertext; } sum.to_bytes() } ``` - `FHEProcessorInput` has got two fields. `ciphertexts` yields `(Vec, u64)` pairs one at a time: the serialised ciphertext and its input index. `params` holds the BFV parameters of the E3. - `Ciphertext::zero` makes the zero ciphertext, which is where you start from. The `+=` operator then adds each input ciphertext onto it. This addition is homomorphic: the function adds up the hidden values without ever getting a look at them. - `sum.to_bytes()` serialises the encrypted result. - `policy()` returns the input policy. The default policy just uses every published input. The template asks for E3s with the `insecure-512` parameter set. Its plaintext modulus is 100, so every result gets worked out modulo 100. For this tutorial, keep 2 × (a + b) under 100. ## Change the computation ### Stop the stack If you've got `pnpm dev:all` running, hit `Ctrl+C` in its terminal. ### Double the encrypted sum Over in `program/src/lib.rs`, swap the `fhe_processor` function out for this version: ```rust filename="program/src/lib.rs" {9-11} /// Implementation of the CiphertextProcessor function pub fn fhe_processor(fhe_inputs: FHEProcessorInput<'_>) -> Vec { let mut sum = Ciphertext::zero(fhe_inputs.params); for (bytes, _) in fhe_inputs.ciphertexts { let ciphertext = Ciphertext::from_bytes(&bytes, fhe_inputs.params).unwrap(); sum += &ciphertext; } // Add the encrypted sum to itself. The hidden value becomes 2 × (a + b). let doubled = &sum + ∑ doubled.to_bytes() } ``` `&sum + &sum` adds the two ciphertexts and gives you back a new ciphertext. You won't need any new imports for it. ### Update the unit test Down the bottom of `program/src/lib.rs` there's a test that encrypts 3 and 2 and calls `fhe_processor`. Bump the expected value from 5 to 10: ```rust filename="program/src/lib.rs" let tally = Vec::::try_decode(&decrypted, Encoding::poly())?; assert_eq!(tally[0], 10); Ok(()) ``` ### Run the unit test ```bash cargo test -p e3-user-program ``` Cargo should print `test tests::test ... ok`. If the test fails, go back and check your `fhe_processor` against the code in the step before. ### Update the label on the input step In `client/src/pages/steps/EnterInputs.tsx`, track down this line: ```tsx filename="client/src/pages/steps/EnterInputs.tsx" Ready to compute: {input1} + {input2} = ? ``` Change it to: ```tsx filename="client/src/pages/steps/EnterInputs.tsx" Ready to compute: 2 × ({input1} + {input2}) = ? ``` ### Update the label on the results step Then in `client/src/pages/steps/Results.tsx`, track down this line: ```tsx filename="client/src/pages/steps/Results.tsx" { submittedInputs ? `${submittedInputs.input1} + ${submittedInputs.input2} = ${result !== null ? result : '…'}` : '…' } ``` Change it to: ```tsx filename="client/src/pages/steps/Results.tsx" { submittedInputs ? `2 × (${submittedInputs.input1} + ${submittedInputs.input2}) = ${result !== null ? result : '…'}` : '…' } ``` ### Start the stack ```bash pnpm dev:all ``` The `PROGRAM` process runs `interfold program start`. In dev mode that command runs `cargo run --bin e3-support-scripts-dev`, so Cargo rebuilds the program server with your new `fhe_processor` in it. ### Run an E3 Open [http://localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000). If the client's still showing the result of an earlier E3, select **Start over** up in the top bar. Request an E3, then punch in 5 and 3. On the input step you'll see `Ready to compute: 2 × (5 + 3) = ?`, and on the results step, `2 × (5 + 3) = 16`. Job done. ## Why nothing else changes - **The contract.** `MyProgram.publishInput` stores a commitment for each input, and `MyProgram.verify` checks the compute proof. The computation isn't in either of them. - **The coordination server.** `server/index.ts` passes every published input on to the program server and publishes whatever output comes back. It hasn't got a clue what the computation does. - **The deployment.** Every time it starts, `pnpm dev:all` deploys the contracts again on a fresh local chain. In dev mode, the program server runs `fhe_processor` without a proof, and the template deploys `MockOpenVmReceiptVerifier`, which waves through every receipt on the local chain. Once you're on real proofs, though, `MyProgram.verify` checks the OpenVM receipt against the `imageId` that `MyProgram` gets when it's deployed. Change the program and you change that identity, so compile and deploy again. Have a look at [Compute provider](/build/e3-program/compute-provider). ## Update the integration test There's an end-to-end test in the template too, in `tests/integration.spec.ts`. It encrypts 1 and 2 and expects their sum, so now you've made your change, update the expected value: ```ts filename="tests/integration.spec.ts" expect(BigInt(result)).toBe(2n * (num1 + num2)) ``` Run the test with `pnpm test:integration`. Heads up: this test needs a CLI that's built with the `test-only-skip-proof-aggregation` Cargo feature, and the release binaries don't come with it. Have a look at [Installation](/build/installation#install-the-cli) for a source build. ## Operations on ciphertexts The template uses the `fhe` crate from `gnosisguild/fhe.rs` at tag `v0.4.2`. For a `Ciphertext`, here's the operators that crate implements: | Operation | Operator | Example | | --------------------------- | -------------------- | ----------------- | | Add two ciphertexts | `+`, `+=` | `&a + &b` | | Subtract two ciphertexts | `-`, `-=` | `&a - &b` | | Negate a ciphertext | unary `-` | `-&a` | | Add or subtract a plaintext | `+`, `+=`, `-`, `-=` | `&a + &plaintext` | | Multiply by a plaintext | `*`, `*=` | `&a * &plaintext` | A `Plaintext` has to use the very same parameters object as the ciphertext, that's `fhe_inputs.params`. If the parameters objects don't match, the operator panics. Every result wraps modulo the plaintext modulus. So a negative result, say from `&a - &b` with `a < b`, wraps round to a big value. The crate implements `*` for two ciphertexts as well, but the default template doesn't use it, and we won't go into it on this page. ## Next steps Write the FHE computation for your own E3 program. Validate inputs and verify proofs in your E3 program contract. Find the file to edit for each part of the template.
